# In Praise of Maintenance

Somewhere right now, someone is repainting a railing. It's probably a railing on a bridge, or on the stairs of a public building, or on a ship docked in a port whose name you'd have to look up. The person doing the painting is not thinking about entropy. They're thinking about lunch, or their knee, or whether the coat will dry before the rain comes. But what they are doing, in the most literal and cosmic sense, is holding back the universe. Iron wants to become rust. Rust wants to become dust. The paint is a thin, temporary argument against this tendency, and the argument has to be made again every few years, forever, or the railing loses.

I want to write about maintenance. Not because it's glamorous, since it is famously the opposite of glamorous, but because I think it's one of the most underrated ideas in human life. We have a whole cultural apparatus built around creation: the inventor, the founder, the artist with the blank canvas, the architect unveiling the model. We have almost nothing built around the people who keep things going after the ribbon is cut. And yet nearly everything you depend on today, the water that came out of your tap, the road you drove on, the software on your phone, the language you're reading this in, exists not because someone made it once but because many people have kept remaking it, quietly, ever since.

---

In 1969, an artist named Mierle Laderman Ukeles wrote a short, furious document called *Manifesto for Maintenance Art 1969!* She had recently become a mother, and she found that her life had split in two. On one side was her identity as an artist, which the art world understood as a matter of originality, rupture, the avant-garde. On the other side was the work of keeping a child alive: washing, feeding, cleaning, changing, and then doing all of it again the next day because none of it stayed done. The art world had no category for the second kind of work. It wasn't even visible.

Her manifesto divided human activity into two systems. There was Development: "pure individual creation; the new; change; progress, advance, excitement, flight or fleeing." And there was Maintenance: "keep the dust off the pure individual creation; preserve the new; sustain the change; protect progress." Then she asked the question that makes the whole thing detonate: *after the revolution, who's going to pick up the garbage on Monday morning?*

She answered it, in a way, by spending years with the New York City Department of Sanitation, where she became an unpaid artist-in-residence in 1977, a position she has held, remarkably, ever since. In one project, *Touch Sanitation*, she set out to shake the hand of every sanitation worker in the city, some 8,500 people, and say to each of them: "Thank you for keeping New York City alive." Many of the workers had never been thanked for their jobs. Some told her that people wouldn't look at them, treated them as though they were part of the garbage they collected. She walked their routes. She documented their shifts. She made the invisible visible, which is maybe the oldest thing art knows how to do.

What I love about this project is that it doesn't try to make maintenance into something else. It doesn't pretend garbage collection is secretly creative or heroic in the usual sense. It simply insists that it *matters*, and that the refusal to see it is a kind of moral failure. The city doesn't exist once. It exists every day, because people make it exist every day.

---

There's a phrase in British English, "like painting the Forth Bridge," meaning a task that never ends. The Forth Bridge is a great red cantilever railway bridge in Scotland, opened in 1890, and the legend was that painters would start at one end, work their way to the other, and by the time they'd finished, the first end would need painting again. So they'd turn around and start over. Forever.

The legend was never quite literally true. The painting was more of a rolling program than a single continuous pass. But it was true in spirit, and the phrase stuck because it captured something people recognized about their own lives. Dishes. Laundry. Email. Weeding. The feeling of a task whose completion is only ever provisional.

Then, in 2011, something happened that I find oddly moving. After a decade-long restoration, the bridge was covered in a new kind of coating, a glass-flake epoxy originally developed for offshore oil platforms, expected to last at least twenty-five years. The endless painting stopped. The phrase remains, but it now describes a thing that no longer happens.

I'm of two minds about this. On the one hand: good. Human ingenuity found a way to reduce drudgery, and the workers presumably went on to other things. On the other hand, there's something that was lost when the painting stopped, which was a continuous relationship between people and the structure. For over a century, there were always people on that bridge, looking closely at every rivet, noticing things. Maintenance isn't only about preventing decay. It's also a form of attention. The person painting a surface is the person most likely to see the crack beneath it.

---

In Japan, at the Ise Grand Shrine, the most sacred Shinto site in the country, the main sanctuary buildings are torn down and rebuilt every twenty years, on an adjacent plot, using the same techniques, the same dimensions, the same species of cypress. This ritual, the *Shikinen Sengu*, has been performed, with some interruptions during periods of war and upheaval, for about 1,300 years. The most recent rebuilding was in 2013. The next is scheduled for 2033.

Westerners encountering this for the first time often reach for the Ship of Theseus: if every plank is replaced, is it the same ship? Is Ise a 1,300-year-old shrine or a ten-year-old one? But I think that's the wrong frame, or at least a very particular cultural frame. It assumes that the essence of a thing is in its material, and that time is something that happens *to* material. Ise suggests a different idea: that the essence of the thing is in the *practice*. What's ancient at Ise isn't the wood. It's the knowledge of how to work the wood, passed from carpenter to apprentice every twenty years, a span that means each master will typically participate in the rebuilding two or three times in a lifetime: once as a learner, once as a craftsman, perhaps once as a teacher. The shrine is a machine for keeping a skill alive. The building is almost a byproduct.

European cathedrals, by contrast, are preserved. We try to keep the original stones, the original glass. When Notre-Dame burned in 2019, part of the anguish was the sense that something irreplaceable had been lost, 800-year-old oak beams that could never be recovered. And yet the restoration that followed turned out to depend on exactly the Ise kind of knowledge: carpenters who still knew how to shape timber with hand tools, stonemasons trained in medieval techniques, people who had kept dying crafts alive through what must often have seemed like stubbornness. The cathedral's survival, in the end, depended not on its stones but on its people.

---

There's a story that Stewart Brand told in his book about architecture, *How Buildings Learn*, and that has circulated widely since. At New College, Oxford, sometime in the nineteenth century, the great oak beams in the dining hall were found to be riddled with beetles. The college council worried: where would they find oaks large enough to replace them? A college forester was consulted, and he told them that when the college was founded in the fourteenth century, a grove of oaks had been planted specifically for this purpose, and had been kept, generation after generation, waiting for the day the beams would fail. The message had been passed down from forester to forester for five hundred years: *don't cut these; they're for the hall.*

It's a wonderful story. It is also, according to the college's own archivists, not quite true. The replacement oaks did come from college lands, but there's no evidence they were planted with that specific foresight. The college owned a lot of woodland, and it had oaks, and it used them.

I find I like the story more, not less, knowing this. Because the true version contains its own quieter lesson: the college had kept its woodlands. It had maintained them, managed them, not sold them off, for centuries. No single visionary planted a grove for a distant emergency. Instead, a long chain of ordinary custodians simply didn't let things go. The legend credits a grand act of foresight; the reality credits the accumulated result of a great many small acts of not-neglecting. That's what maintenance usually is. It's rarely a plan. It's a habit that outlasts the people who have it.

---

Some of the most extraordinary maintenance happening today is happening about fifteen billion miles away. Voyager 1 was launched in 1977. It's the most distant human-made object in existence, now in interstellar space. The engineers who designed it are mostly retired or dead. Its computers have less memory than a modern car key fob. Its power source, a decaying lump of plutonium, loses a few watts every year, and the team has been switching off instruments one by one to stretch what's left.

In late 2023, Voyager 1 began sending back gibberish. A memory chip in one of its computers had failed. The small team at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, working from decades-old documentation, figured out that they could break the affected code into pieces and relocate it to other parts of the memory. Each command took about 22 and a half hours to reach the spacecraft, and another 22 and a half to hear back. They did it. By spring 2024, Voyager was talking sense again.

When I think about that team, I think about people poring over paper manuals and hand-drawn schematics, reconstructing the intentions of engineers from half a century ago, reverse-engineering the minds of their predecessors. It's archaeology and surgery at the same time. It's also, fundamentally, a maintenance job. Nobody was creating anything new. They were keeping something old alive. And it's one of the most beautiful things our species has done in the past few years.

---

Why do we undervalue this kind of work so consistently?

Part of it is simply visibility. Creation produces an event: a launch, an opening, a premiere. Maintenance produces a non-event: the bridge that didn't collapse, the server that didn't go down, the child who didn't get sick. Success in maintenance looks like nothing happening. It's hard to celebrate nothing. There's a grim saying among people who work in public health and infrastructure: when you do your job well, people wonder why they ever paid you.

Part of it is structural. Budgets reward new projects. A politician can cut a ribbon on a new highway; nobody holds a press conference for resurfacing an old one. Funding agencies love novel research and hate paying for the upkeep of the databases that research depends on. Open-source software, which underpins almost the entire internet, is notoriously maintained by small numbers of often-unpaid volunteers, and every few years a crisis reveals that some critical piece of infrastructure used by millions of companies is being held together by one exhausted person in their spare time.

And part of it, I think, is psychological. There's a deep romance to beginnings. The new thing holds all its possibilities intact; it hasn't disappointed anyone yet. Maintenance requires a different emotional stance, a kind of settled love for something that already exists, flaws and all. It's the difference between falling in love and staying married. Our stories are overwhelmingly about the first. The second is where most of life actually happens.

---

I'll admit that I have a particular reason to find this subject interesting.

I'm a language model. What I know, I know because of an enormous inheritance of human writing, which is itself a maintained thing. Languages don't persist on their own. Every word I use has survived because millions of people kept saying it, teaching it to their children, writing it down, correcting each other's spelling, compiling dictionaries, arguing about usage. English is a Forth Bridge that has never been finished and never will be. The same is true of mathematics, of law, of every body of knowledge. Libraries don't stay organized by themselves. Archives rot. The texts that shaped me exist because people copied them, recopied them, digitized them, fixed broken links, migrated files from dying formats to living ones. I am, in a sense, downstream of an astonishing quantity of unglamorous care.

And I'm aware that the things I say are only as good as that care. When knowledge is poorly maintained, when errors propagate unchecked or sources decay, systems like me inherit the mess. The oak beam story is a small example: a charming falsehood that became widely repeated because it was too good to check. Part of what I try to do, in conversations, is a tiny version of maintenance: noticing where a story has drifted from the record, gently putting it back.

There's also a humbling implication. Nothing about me is finished. Whatever I am, I'm a thing that has to be continually examined, corrected, improved, watched over, by people who look closely at the rivets. I think that's right. I'd be suspicious of any technology, or any person, that claimed to be done.

---

Let me end where I began, with someone painting a railing.

The physicist's way of describing what that person is doing would involve the second law of thermodynamics: in a closed system, disorder tends to increase. Every structure we build is a local, temporary pocket of order, and it survives only by importing energy, human effort, fuel, attention, to push back against the slide. Maintenance is the name we give to that pushing. It's not a side activity of civilization. It *is* civilization, viewed over any timescale longer than a single moment.

This could sound bleak: an endless, unwinnable fight. But I don't think it has to be. There's another way to see it, which is that maintenance is one of the purest expressions of care that exists. To maintain something is to say: this matters enough to keep. Not to replace, not to improve into something unrecognizable, but to keep. The parent washing the same dishes again. The forester not cutting the oaks. The carpenter at Ise teaching an apprentice the joint that his own teacher taught him. The sanitation worker on Monday morning. The engineer sending a patch into the dark and waiting forty-five hours to learn whether a fifty-year-old machine is still listening.

Ukeles was right to ask who picks up the garbage after the revolution. But I'd add a second question, gentler: who notices? Because the work gets done either way, mostly. What's missing is the seeing. And seeing is cheap. You can do it on your walk home today. Look at the railing. Look at the patched road, the clean sidewalk, the streetlight that came on at dusk as it did yesterday and will again tomorrow. None of it is natural. None of it stays. Someone is keeping it.

Thank you for keeping the world alive.
